clue.text: Howl from greedy types at invasion site

parts.note: to howl like a hound is to bay
greedy people are called pigs, so something from them is 'of pigs'

explanation.surface: A protest erupts from grasping people at the spot where troops landed.
explanation.walkthrough: The Bay of Pigs in Cuba was where US-backed exiles made a failed landing in 1961.
explanation.definitionFit: The 1961 Cuban landing by US-backed exiles took place at this inlet, making it a famous invasion location.

clue.text: Pilot light's first to go in most enormous short

indicators.note: going in means being placed inside the shortened word
short means cut off at the end, losing the final letter

parts.note: biggest means most enormous

indicators.note: first means only the opening letter of light is used

explanation.surface: A pilot light goes out first in the largest heater, which shorts.
explanation.walkthrough: 'short' cuts BIGGEST to BIGGES; 'first' takes L from 'light's'; 'to go in' puts it inside. Biggles is the fictional flying ace of W. E. Johns's boys' books.
explanation.definitionFit: Captain W. E. Johns's hero is a fictional airman, an RAF flier.

clue.text: Molly has this last word? That's right

definitions.meaning: Molly Bloom's monologue closes James Joyce's Ulysses on an affirmation
an assent, a word of agreement

explanation.walkthrough: Molly Bloom's soliloquy ends Joyce's Ulysses with 'yes'.
explanation.definitionFit: Joyce's novel ends with Molly Bloom's affirmation, and the same word is a plain affirmative reply.

clue.text: Once in favour of just ignoring a European

parts.note: for means in favour of

indicators.note: ignoring means leaving out, so the letter is removed

parts.note: merely means just
E is the abbreviation for European

explanation.surface: Previously supporting someone just because they weren't from Europe.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Once' sits at the front looking like an adverb of the surface; 'ignoring' drops the European from 'just', and 'a European' is a single letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Once in the sense 'at one time in the past' means previously.

clue.text: In short, almost suffer

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: almost means one letter short, so the end is dropped

parts.note: curt means short, brusque

explanation.surface: To put it briefly, nearly endure.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In short' reads as 'briefly', but 'In' is taken literally and 'short' is the synonym that 'almost' trims by its final letter.
explanation.definitionFit: To incur a loss is to sustain or undergo it.

clue.text: Dance bands are a disaster

indicators.note: a disaster is a mess, so the letters are scrambled

explanation.surface: Musical groups make a hash of things.
explanation.walkthrough: 'disaster' rearranges the letters of 'bands are a'.
explanation.definitionFit: A stately Spanish triple-time court movement, common in Baroque suites.

clue.text: Warning British prime minister to retire

indicators.note: retiring means drawing back, so the statesman's name is read backwards here

parts.note: Sir Robert Peel was a nineteenth-century British prime minister

explanation.surface: A notice that a British premier is about to step down.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to retire' is the reversal signal: the premier is the Victorian Robert Peel, whose name runs backwards after the British abbreviation.
explanation.definitionFit: An electronic beep or alarm tone serves as an alert signal.

clue.text: What may lie ahead largely for VIP?

parts.note: big means large
read as 'a head', a wig is what may lie on a head

explanation.surface: What awaits a very important person, largely?
explanation.walkthrough: 'ahead' splits into 'a head', where a wig sits.
explanation.definitionFit: A bigwig is an important person, a big shot.

clue.text: Infer perhaps wide dish is empty?

parts.note: in cricket a wide is an extra, a run not scored off the bat

indicators.note: here 'is' links the dish with what it holds, nothing, so the O sits inside it

parts.note: a plate is a dish
empty means containing nothing, and O is nothing

explanation.surface: Can you infer that a large dish is bare?
explanation.walkthrough: A wide is a cricket extra. 'dish is empty' means a plate with nothing (O) inside, P(O)LATE.
explanation.definitionFit: To extrapolate is to infer by extending known data, so inferring is one example.

clue.text: Most colourful stuff from pen produced in pain

indicators.note: produced in means placed inside the nuisance word

parts.note: a pest is a pain, a nuisance
ink flows from a pen

explanation.surface: Bright writing fluid comes out of a pen while in agony.
explanation.walkthrough: 'pain' is a person who annoys, not physical hurt; 'produced in' sets the pen's fluid inside that nuisance.
explanation.definitionFit: Pink here means rosiest, the most brightly flushed in hue.

clue.text: Air-con said to produce a type of 'flu

indicators.note: said tells us the phrase is spoken, giving a word that sounds the same

parts.note: air is GAS and a con is a TRICK, giving 'gas trick'

explanation.surface: An air-conditioning unit is blamed for spreading an illness.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Air-con' looks like air conditioning, but splits into air (GAS) and con (TRICK); 'said' turns 'gas trick' into the stomach word.
explanation.definitionFit: Gastric flu is the everyday name for a stomach bug, so the adjective names a kind of influenza.

clue.text: Excellent king — nothing wrong with withholding name

parts.note: R, for Rex, is the usual abbreviation for king

indicators.note: wrong signals that the letters are put in a different order

parts.note: the word as written gives the letters to shuffle

explanation.surface: A fine monarch, with nothing amiss, keeps his name secret.
explanation.walkthrough: 'with withholding name' takes one N away; 'wrong' then rearranges the six letters left (OTHING) behind the king's letter.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is an informal exclamation of approval, much like 'spot on' or 'great'.

clue.text: Philosopher doesn't quite make case for his portrait

indicators.note: falling just short means the final letter of the trinket word is dropped

parts.note: a locket is a small case holding a picture of a loved one

explanation.surface: A thinker is not quite able to build a frame for his own picture.
explanation.walkthrough: 'doesn't quite make' cuts the last letter off LOCKET.
explanation.definitionFit: John Locke was the seventeenth-century English thinker behind empiricism.

clue.text: Find directions here to limit wine

parts.note: to compass is to encircle or confine
rosé is a pink wine

explanation.surface: Locate guidance on restricting your drinking.
explanation.walkthrough: A compass rose is the star-shaped card on a map or compass showing the cardinal points.
explanation.definitionFit: The marked dial on charts shows north, south, east and west, so bearings are read from it.

clue.text: Foreign letter-writer with block turns to collection of teachers

indicators.note: turns tells us the whole string of pieces is read backwards

parts.note: eta is a letter of the Greek alphabet
a nib is the writing tip of a pen
to bar is to block

explanation.surface: An overseas correspondent with writer's block switches to a group of instructors.
explanation.walkthrough: 'letter-writer' looks like one word but splits; 'turns' reverses ETANIBBAR as a whole.
explanation.definitionFit: A rabbi is a Jewish religious teacher, and this collective noun names rabbis as a body.

clue.text: Ass went regularly through tunnel

indicators.note: one thing going through another sits inside it, so the picked letters sit within the tunnel

parts.note: the Simplon is a long railway tunnel through the Alps between Switzerland and Italy

indicators.note: taking letters at regular intervals from the word went yields its second and fourth

explanation.surface: A donkey trotted steadily through an underground passage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'regularly' takes E and T from 'went'; 'through' puts them inside SIMPLON.
explanation.definitionFit: Calling someone an ass means they are a fool, a gullible dimwit.

clue.text: About time princess got up? Say damn (but not blast)

indicators.note: in a down clue, getting up means reading from the bottom upwards
about means going round, so the princess's name surrounds the time letter

parts.note: Princess Margaret, the late sister of Queen Elizabeth II

explanation.surface: Was the princess rising late? Use a mild swear word, but not a strong one.
explanation.walkthrough: 'About' puts T inside MARGARET, and 'got up' reverses MARGARTET. Damn has four letters and blast five.
explanation.definitionFit: A word of four letters; damn qualifies while blast, with five, does not.

clue.text: Government check closes a defensive construction

indicators.note: closing around something means enclosing it, so the test's letters wrap the A

parts.note: the MOT is the annual British vehicle roadworthiness test, named after the Ministry of Transport

explanation.surface: A state inspection shuts down a fortification.
explanation.walkthrough: 'closes' puts A inside MOT, the yearly British car safety test.
explanation.definitionFit: A water-filled ditch around a castle served as a barrier against attackers.

clue.text: Show one's anxious for each pointer to heaven

parts.note: per means for each
a church spire points skyward

explanation.surface: Each church steeple appears nervous.
explanation.walkthrough: Sweating is a sign of nerves.
explanation.definitionFit: Breaking into a sweat is a physical sign of nerves or worry.

clue.text: Toby doesn't have to exert unfair influence

indicators.note: lacking the little word means it is taken out of the full name

parts.note: Toby is a pet form of the name Tobias
the word as written gives the letters removed

explanation.surface: A man named Toby need not apply pressure unfairly.
explanation.walkthrough: Toby is short for Tobias; 'doesn't have' takes TO out of TOBIAS.
explanation.definitionFit: To prejudice or slant a judgment is to sway it improperly.

clue.text: Nasty woman pins two partners in entrance

indicators.note: to pin is to hold fast, so the partners sit inside the insult

parts.note: a bitch is an insulting word for a spiteful woman
in bridge, East and West are partners

explanation.surface: A spiteful woman catches a couple in the doorway.
explanation.walkthrough: 'entrance' is the verb (to charm), not a door. East and West form one bridge partnership.
explanation.definitionFit: To entrance as a verb is to enchant or cast a spell over.

clue.text: The target broken by record number of day-trippers here

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: being broken by something means having it inserted, so the record splits the target

parts.note: a mark is something aimed at
an EP is an extended-play record

explanation.surface: A target is shattered by a record-breaking crowd of tourists.
explanation.walkthrough: 'record' looks like a feat to be broken, but it is a short vinyl disc; 'broken by' sets it inside the target word.
explanation.definitionFit: An amusement venue such as Alton Towers draws crowds of visitors for a single day out.

clue.text: Diarist in skirt, extremely short

indicators.note: in means placed inside the skirt word

parts.note: a kilt is a Scottish skirt

indicators.note: short means the final letter is lopped off

parts.note: very means extremely

explanation.surface: A diary writer wearing a very short skirt.
explanation.walkthrough: 'short' trims the last letter of the word for 'extremely', and 'in' puts what remains inside the Scottish garment. Francis Kilvert was a Victorian clergyman whose diaries are famous.
explanation.definitionFit: Francis Kilvert, a Victorian curate, kept a celebrated journal of rural life.

clue.text: From island, blog at intervals, visiting not so much

indicators.note: a visitor goes in, so the picked letters sit inside the word for fewer

parts.note: less means not so much

indicators.note: at intervals means taking alternate letters, the first and third of blog

explanation.surface: Someone posting from an island blogs only occasionally, visiting less often.
explanation.walkthrough: 'at intervals' takes B and O from 'blog'; 'visiting' puts them inside LESS.
explanation.definitionFit: Lesbos is a large Greek isle in the Aegean, home of the poet Sappho.

clue.text: Dawn's late breaking in desert

indicators.note: breaking means smashing up, so these letters are rearranged

parts.note: the possessive s is kept here as a letter of the fodder
taken as written

explanation.surface: Daybreak arrives late in an arid region.
explanation.walkthrough: 'breaking' rearranges DAWNS and LATE; the possessive S counts as a letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A barren desolate expanse is the same as an arid tract of land.

clue.text: Wasted down here-that could be nadir

indicators.note: could be signals the letters may become something else, a rearrangement

explanation.surface: Squandered at rock bottom: that might be the lowest point.
explanation.walkthrough: 'could be' rearranges NADIR. Money that goes down the drain is wasted.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom 'down the drain' means lost or squandered, so the drain is where wasted things go.

clue.text: Dandy title in part for Shakespeare, after all

indicators.note: after the word all means only what follows it in the title is kept

parts.note: the start of the play title All's Well That Ends Well
the word as written gives the letters removed

explanation.surface: A fop takes a part in a Shakespeare play, after all.
explanation.walkthrough: 'after' keeps what follows ALL in 'All's Well That Ends Well'.
explanation.definitionFit: A swell is old slang for a fashionable, smartly dressed gentleman.

clue.text: Perhaps saw almost plain row of buttons

parts.note: a saw is one example of a tool

indicators.note: almost means one letter short, so the last letter is dropped

parts.note: plain can mean bare, unadorned

explanation.surface: A simple sawing job may leave a plain line of fasteners.
explanation.walkthrough: 'saw' looks like a verb or a proverb, but it is one example of a tool; 'almost' trims the last letter of the word for 'plain'.
explanation.definitionFit: On a computer screen, a strip of clickable icons runs along the window.

clue.text: Song and dance alternately for Strauss role

parts.note: an aria is a solo song in opera

indicators.note: alternately means taking every other letter, so the first, third and fifth of dance

explanation.surface: Singing and dancing take turns in a part by an Austrian composer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'alternately' takes D, N, E from 'dance'.
explanation.definitionFit: Richard Strauss wrote the opera Ariadne auf Naxos, whose title heroine is a major soprano part.

clue.text: Couple manage to stay united

indicators.note: to stay can mean to detain or hold, so the manage word holds the letter

parts.note: to do is to manage, as in 'we'll make do'
U is the abbreviation for United, as in football club names

explanation.surface: A pair manage to remain together.
explanation.walkthrough: Stay in the sense 'detain' makes DO hold U.
explanation.definitionFit: A duo is a pair, two people working together.

clue.text: Car won't start — take to these?

indicators.note: not starting means the first letter is missing

parts.note: wheels is slang for a car

explanation.surface: The car won't go, so run away on foot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'won't start' drops the W from WHEELS. To 'take to your heels' is to run away.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom to take to one's heels means to run off, so these are what you flee on.

clue.text: Chap has to leave something on the plate

parts.note: a chap is a man
to get out is to leave

explanation.surface: A man must go, leaving food uneaten.
explanation.walkthrough: MANGETOUT is a flat pea pod eaten whole, the snow pea.
explanation.definitionFit: This pea, eaten in its pod, is a vegetable served with a meal.
